thread.title: Why Starbucks' Reaction To Schultz's Resignation Was Muted

author: Martin Tillier
title: Why Starbucks' Reaction To Schultz's Resignation Was Muted
text:
Shutterstock photo
Yesterday, Howard Schultz, the founder and face of Starbucks ( SBUX ) announced that he is leaving the company completely. The initial market reaction was exactly what you would expect: the stock plummeted in the minute following the announcement. Less than ten minutes later, however, SBUX was back to where it started.
For many people, I’m sure that was confusing. Schultz has, after all, built a conspicuous personal brand that has him as the visionary leader of the company. That image has continued recently, even though he stepped down as CEO last year, so it would seem to be logical to regard his departure as a negative for the stock.
In this case, there is an underlying logic to the market’s reaction that makes the bounce back the move that makes sense.
First and foremost, although the timing was a surprise, the decision itself was not. From the minute Schultz announced that he was stepping down as CEO in December of 2016, there has been speculation that he would leave completely. The stock’s limited reaction and immediate retracement shows that the market had already taken that speculation seriously.
Secondly, the market has learned over the years that once a company achieves a certain critical mass, the loss of an icon is not a reason to sell the stock. There are numerous examples that prove that, but let’s look at two great American multinational companies that prove the point.
McDonald's
Ray Kroc was not technically the founder of McDonald’s ( MCD ) but he was the person that built it into by far the world’s largest restaurant chain. When he died in January of 1984, MCD dropped nearly fifteen percent to the equivalent of $2.38, even though in his later years he seemed more concerned with running his beloved San Diego Padres than the restaurant empire that made him rich.
One year later, MCD was thirty percent higher and of course his passing did not, as was posited at the time, mark the high-water mark for the company. The stock hit a high of $178.70 a few months ago.
Apple
By the time we got to Steve Jobs’ resignation as CEO of Apple ( AAPL ) in August of 2011, traders and investors had learned that no matter how much an individual is connected to a brand, the company is bigger than any individual. Even though Jobs had enhanced his reputation after his return to Apple, the stock barely registered his resignation and was trading higher than before he left just a few days later.
In this case too, the opinion that Jobs’ absence signaled a turning point for Apple was voiced many times over the next couple of years. A glance Apple's chart shows that not to be the case .
It is often said of iconic visionaries and leaders such as Kroc, Jobs, and Schultz that the companies they build are their babies, and if you think in those terms, the reason that growth usually continues long after they are gone is obvious. Anybody who is a parent knows that at some point you must entrust your child’s care to someone else, and we all do so only when we completely trust that person or group of people to nurture them and look after them.
CEOs treat their babies no differently. When Schultz resigned as CEO, Kevin Johnson was appointed as his successor and, given Johnson’s tech background, Schultz evidently felt that his baby would continue to grow under his care.
Despite that noticeable recovery yesterday, SBUX is trading a little lower today as fund managers make their adjustments to the news. That downward momentum may continue for a while so I would not jump in yet, but if the losses extend below $55, or if there is any sign of a bounce, I would regard the stock as a buy on the basis that the departure or loss of an icon usually means less than people think it will.
